summary: Defines the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF), a data format that incident response teams use to share information about computer security incidents. It gives an information model and an XML Schema data model. It was replaced by RFC 7970.

plainLanguage.summary: When a security team sees an attack that involves another organisation, it needs to tell that organisation what it saw. IODEF is a shared vocabulary for such reports, written as XML so that machines can read it and people can process it quickly. It covers the systems involved, how the attack worked, how much damage it did, and what the sender would like the receiver to do about it.

subtitle: A common XML format for the incident reports that security teams exchange with each other.

tldr.problem: Organisations often need help from other parties to deal with malicious activity, whether that means asking an ISP to filter attack traffic, asking a remote site to shut down a bot network, or sharing a list of known bad addresses. The information was exchanged in whatever format each team preferred.
tldr.mechanism: IODEF defines an information model for an incident, covering hosts, networks, services, attack methods, forensic records, impact and requested actions, and expresses it as an XML document with a published XML Schema.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5070 is a Proposed Standard from December 2007 and has been obsoleted by RFC 7970, which restates the format and separates the information model from the guidance for its use.

facts.label: Purpose values
facts.value: traceback, mitigation, reporting, other and an escape value

today: RFC 5070 is a Proposed Standard from December 2007, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7970, which restates the Incident Object Description Exchange Format. The RFC itself describes the format as serving as a transport format whose specific representation is not the best one for on-disk storage, long-term archiving or in-memory processing.

sections.title: Why Incident Response Teams Need a Common Format
sections.content:
Organisations need help from other parties to mitigate malicious activity and to gain insight into potential threats. That coordination might mean working with an ISP to filter attack traffic, contacting a remote site to take down a bot network, or sharing watch-lists of known malicious addresses within a consortium.

IODEF is a format for representing the computer security information that incident response teams commonly exchange. It gives an XML representation for conveying incident information across administrative domains, between parties that have an operational responsibility for remediation or for watching out over a defined constituency. The data model encodes information about hosts, networks and the services running on them, about attack methodology and the associated forensic evidence, about the impact of the activity, and about limited ways of documenting workflow.

The overriding purpose is to improve the operational capability of the teams that use it. Community adoption means incidents can be resolved and situational awareness conveyed more easily. A structured format lets incident data be processed automatically, which saves analysts from parsing free-form documents; it reduces the effort of normalising similar data from different sources; and it gives a common basis for interoperable tools, particularly when the data comes from several constituencies.

The RFC is careful about what it does not cover. Coordinating with other teams is not only a technical problem, and there are procedural, trust and legal considerations that may stop an organisation sharing anything at all. IODEF does not attempt to address those, though implementations have to take them into account.
sections.plainLanguage: Every security team writes its incident reports differently, so the other team has to read them by hand. IODEF fixes a common structure so that the same facts can be written once and read by any tool.

sections.title: The Incident Class and Its Parts
sections.content:
Every IODEF document is an instance of the IODEF-Document class, which has three attributes: a version that must be 1.00, a language code, and an optional free-form format identifier whose meaning must be negotiated out of band. It contains one or more Incident elements.

Each Incident holds an incident tracking number from the team that produced the document, optionally the tracking numbers other teams use for the same incident, the times the incident was detected, started, ended and reported, free-form descriptions, one or more assessments of the impact, the methods the intruder used, contact details for the parties involved, and any event data. It also carries a restriction attribute that states the disclosure guidelines the sender expects the receiver to follow, with four values: public for no restrictions, need-to-know for sharing only with others involved in the incident, private for no sharing, and default for sharing under a policy the parties have already arranged. The default for the Incident class is private, and the value is inherited by the child classes, which may tighten or relax it.

The RFC states that this restriction attribute provides no security in itself, because there is no technical means of forcing the recipient to honour it. It is guidance, and enforcement is not a technical problem the format can solve.
sections.plainLanguage: An incident record holds a reference number, the times it was detected, started, ended and reported, an assessment of the damage, how the attack was done, and who to contact. It also carries a disclosure label, which the sender sets and the receiver may ignore.

sections.title: Encoding, Namespace and Validation
sections.content:
Every IODEF document must begin with an XML declaration and must state the XML version. If UTF-8 is not used, the character encoding must also be given. The characters that have special meaning in XML must be written as entity references: the ampersand, the less-than sign, the greater-than sign, the double quotation mark and the apostrophe.

The schema declares the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-1.0, and each document should include a valid reference to the schema. Documents must be well-formed XML and should be validated against the schema in Section 8 of the RFC.

The RFC warns that passing the schema is not the same as being semantically valid. Several rules in the text of Section 3 cannot easily be encoded in the schema and a parser has to check them as well. Elements declared as postal address, name, phone and email types are plain strings in the schema but have stricter formatting in the text; a language value has to be checked against the list of possible values; a currency attribute has to be checked against the list of valid currencies; at least one of the Contact and EventData classes must be present even though the schema makes both optional; a parser must accept reports that leave out the node role and software fields; and the enumerated ports of a port list have to be symmetrical between sources and targets.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is XML in a namespace of its own, and a parser should check it against the published schema. The schema alone is not enough: several rules are only written out in prose and a program has to enforce them too.

sections.title: Extending the Model
sections.content:
The RFC offers two ways to extend IODEF. The first is to extend the enumerated values of an attribute, such as the purpose or the restriction, using the escape values the model provides for that purpose. The second is to extend the classes themselves.

The RFC sets out the rules for extending a class. An extension must be defined in a separate specification, and it must declare a distinct namespace so that it can be told apart from the core model. The extended element is placed in the AdditionalData element, which carries the name of the specification, the type of the data, an offset into that specification where the definition starts, and the meaning of the data. The same mechanism is used for the record items inside a forensic record, where the extension describes how the enclosed text should be interpreted.

The RFC also says what an extension must not do. It must not change the meaning of any existing element, and it must not contradict the core model. Extensions are meant to carry information that is specific to one organisation or one community without disturbing the common core that lets two teams interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Teams sometimes need to record something the standard does not cover. The format allows extra elements, but each one has to live in its own namespace and be described separately, so that a reader can tell which parts are standard and which are local.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives four worked examples. The first is a report of an instance of the Code Red worm. It opens an Incident element with the purpose attribute set to reporting, gives an incident identifier with the name of the reporting team and a tracking number, a report time, and a short description. An assessment records that an administrative privilege was attempted and failed. A contact entry names the reporting organisation, gives its registry handle and its email address.

The event data then describes the flow: a source system with an IPv4 address and a counter of 57 events, and a target system with an IPv4 network, both running a service on port 6. An expectation element asks for the offending host to be blocked. A record holds an excerpt from a web server log, with a date and time, a description, and the log line itself, followed by a link to the full log. A history element notes that contact had already been made with the source network owner. The other examples cover reconnaissance, a bot network report and a watch list.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same structure filled in for four situations: a worm spreading, a scan of a network, a bot network and a shared list of addresses. In each, the shape is the same: what happened, to which systems, what the damage was, and what the sender wants done.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the data model itself introduces no security issues, because it only defines a representation. The risk lies in the data. Incident information is often privacy-sensitive for the parties exchanging it and for the parties it describes, so care is needed in disclosing it, both when the document is sent and afterwards. The first of those must be handled by the messaging format; the second has to be addressed by the systems that process, store and archive the documents.

There is a second concern about action. A document may contain a request for action, or a parser may have its own logic to act on what it finds. A parser therefore has to authenticate the recipient of the document and assign an appropriate confidence to the data before acting on it.

The underlying messaging format and protocol must provide confidentiality, integrity and authenticity, and the RFC encourages the use of a standardised security protocol. It points at the Real-time Internetworking Defense protocol and its transport binding of IODEF over SOAP as examples that provide such security. The restriction attribute, described earlier as guidance, is presented here again as a privacy policy the sender suggests, with the same warning that the recipient is free to ignore it and that enforcement is not a technical problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The format itself is not the risk; the contents are. A report may ask the reader to act, so the reader has to know who sent it before it takes any action, and the channel it arrives over has to be confidential and authentic.

root.label: IODEF-Document
root.note: version, lang and an optional formatid

items.label: Traceback
items.desc: The document was sent for trace-back purposes.

items.label: Mitigation
items.desc: The document was sent to request aid in mitigating the described activity.

items.label: Reporting
items.desc: The document was sent to comply with reporting requirements.

items.label: Other
items.desc: The document was sent for purposes specified in the Expectation class.

items.label: Public
items.desc: No restrictions are placed on the information.

items.label: Need to know
items.desc: The information may be shared with other parties involved in the incident.

items.label: Private
items.desc: The information may not be shared. This is the default for the Incident class.

items.label: Default
items.desc: The information can be shared according to a policy agreed between the communicating parties.

data.title: An incident report
data.code:
<Incident purpose="reporting">
  <IncidentID name="csirt.example.com">189493</IncidentID>
  <ReportTime>2001-09-13T23:19:24+00:00</ReportTime>
  <Description>Host sending out Code Red probes</Description>
  <Assessment>
    <Impact completion="failed" type="admin"/>
  </Assessment>
  <Contact role="creator" type="organization">
    <ContactName>Example.com CSIRT</ContactName>
    <RegistryHandle registry="arin">example-com</RegistryHandle>
    <Email>contact@csirt.example.com</Email>
  </Contact>
</Incident>
